0.title: 1 Chronicles — Seek His Face
0.overview:
First Chronicles is not a duplicate of Samuel and Kings — it is a sermon preached to a broken people. The Chronicler writes for a community that has returned from Babylonian exile, standing in the rubble of Jerusalem, asking the question every exiled soul asks: Has God forgotten us? Have his promises failed? Is there still a covenant? The answer the Chronicler gives across twenty-nine chapters is thunderous: No. The covenant has not failed. The throne of David still stands — not in the palace on Ophel, but in the purposes of God. And you, returned remnant, are still his people.

The book divides cleanly in two. Chapters 1–9 are the genealogies — and we must not skip them. These lists are not padding; they are a theological argument. Israel's story is embedded in the story of all humanity, traced from Adam himself. You belong to a line that stretches back to the first man and forward to the eternal King. Chapters 10–29 focus almost entirely on David — but not the David of the bedroom or the battlefield. The Chronicler's David is the man who organized Israel's worship, who carried the ark with joy, who wrote psalms, who assigned the Levites their roles, who gathered materials for the temple, and who charged Solomon with the great task of building a house for the Name of the LORD.

R. C. Sproul once observed that Chronicles is "the Old Testament's most sustained meditation on what it means to be the people of God gathered in worship." That captures it. The governing phrase of the book — "seek the LORD," "seek his face" (16:11; 22:19; 28:9) — is the Chronicler's pastoral word to every discouraged saint in every generation. When the institutions have crumbled, when the temple has been burned, when the exile has scattered the family: seek his face. He is still there. His covenant is still sure. His presence is still the one thing needful.

Christologically, 1 Chronicles is a sustained anticipation of the greater David and the true temple. Every time David says "I cannot build it — there is a man of rest coming after me" (22:9), we hear the echo of John 2:19: "Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up." Jesus Christ is the temple David could only dream of, the King whose throne is truly eternal, the Son of whom the Father said, "I will be his Father, and he shall be my Son" (17:13) — and meant it in a way no merely human king could exhaust. First Chronicles is the gospel in scaffolding.

1.overview:
The book begins where the Bible begins, with the first man, and takes fifty-four verses to reach the edge of Israel. Adam to Noah in ten names (vv. 1-4); the nations spread out from Japheth and Ham (vv. 5-16); the line narrowed through Shem to Abraham (vv. 17-27); Abraham's other sons honoured and set aside (vv. 28-33); Isaac's two sons, and Esau's house given at length (vv. 34-42); and finally the kings and chiefs of Edom (vv. 43-54).

Read as a list it is inert. Read as an answer it is not. The first people to hold this book were a province of Persia with no king, a small temple and a burnt city, and the question they could not put down was whether they were still the people of God at all. The Chronicler answers by opening the register at Adam and letting the line run unbroken through everything that had happened to them.
1.theology:
Two doctrines are carried by the shape of the chapter rather than stated in it. The first is that election narrows without impoverishing: the brothers outside the line are named, honoured and given real futures — twelve princes to Ishmael, a kingdom to Esau — before the text moves on. God's choice of one has never been his abandonment of the rest.

The second is providence at the speed of centuries. Edom is reigning while Israel waits, and the Chronicler writes that down without apology because he is writing after the throne came, and after it went, and after God kept the line alive anyway. A genealogy is the least dramatic form providence takes and one of the most convincing: nobody in it knew what he was part of.
1.examples:
Fifty-four verses of names are the last thing a modern reader wants, and they were the first thing this reader needed, because a name in a register is a fact that does not depend on how he feels about himself. A believer who cannot see what his life has amounted to is in the position of a man in verse 22 — one of Joktan's thirteen sons, no story attached, no deed recorded, and set down in the book of God all the same.

The record is still being kept. It has changed hands and changed form, and the names in it now are written where nothing can burn them: the Lamb's book of life, which is the genealogy this one was always running towards.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The book opens with no sentence at all — a name, and then another. Ten names carry creation to the flood (vv. 1-4); then the world spreads out in the sons of Japheth and Ham, forty-odd peoples covering every coast the first readers knew (vv. 5-16); then the line narrows through Shem to Eber, forks at Peleg and Joktan (vv. 17-23), and walks ten more names to a man whose name God changed: Abram, that is, Abraham (v. 27). Two men in twenty-seven verses are given a note of character, and both notes point at Babel — Nimrod the first mighty man (v. 10) and Peleg, in whose days the earth was divided (v. 19).
verseByVerse.theology: Beginning at Adam rather than at Abraham is a theological decision, not an archival one. Israel is not presented as an alternative to the nations but as a branch of the one human family — which is why the list can run forward to a Gospel that is preached to every nation, and backward, in Luke's hands, to the son of Adam, the son of God.
verseByVerse.examples: A community that has lost everything defines itself by what cannot be confiscated. Land, throne, temple and army had all been taken. The register had not. An empire can burn a palace; it cannot make a man not be his father's son.

verseByVerse.quote: Adam, Seth, Enosh; Kenan, Mahalalel, Jared; Enoch, Methuselah, Lamech; Noah, Shem, Ham, and Japheth.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Nine chapters of names stand between the reader and the first story in this book, and they begin with no sentence at all. Not a word of the LORD coming to anyone, not a creation, not a call. A name, and then another.

Picture the man who first read it. He is in Jerusalem, perhaps four generations after the return from Babylon. The temple he worships in is a smaller building than the one his great-grandfather wept over. There is no king, no army, no border he could defend. Persia decides what happens in his city. He is the subject of an empire that has never heard of him, living in the ruins of a kingdom his neighbours' grandfathers burned.

The question underneath a life like that is not a theological one. It is whether his people are still anybody. And the answer he is handed is not an argument. It is a list — and the list does not begin at Abraham, or at Sinai, or at the throne he no longer has. It begins at the first man God made.

Everything that could be taken from that community had been taken: land, throne, temple, army. What could not be taken was the register. An empire can burn a palace. It cannot make a man not be his father's son.

Which is why Matthew opens his Gospel with a genealogy, and Luke runs the same line the other way — back past David, past Abraham, past Noah, to the son of Adam, the son of God (Luke 3:38). The chain that starts here does not stop at Israel, and it did not stop at the exile.

Ten names from the first man to the flood, and then three sons. No verbs, no deeds. And the God who has kept the record since the first man has not lost one of them.

verseByVerse.quote: The sons of Japheth: Gomer, Magog, Madai, Javan, Tubal, Meshech, and Tiras. The sons of Gomer: Ashkenaz, Riphath, and Togarmah. The sons of Javan: Elishah, Tarshish, Kittim, and Rodanim. The sons of Ham: Cush, Egypt, Put, and Canaan. The sons of Cush: Seba, Havilah, Sabta, Raamah, and Sabteca. The sons of Raamah: Sheba and Dedan. Cush fathered Nimrod. He was the first on earth to be a mighty man. Egypt fathered Ludim, Anamim, Lehabim, Naphtuhim, Pathrusim, Casluhim (from whom the Philistines came), and Caphtorim. Canaan fathered Sidon his firstborn and Heth, and the Jebusites, the Amorites, the Girgashites, the Hivites, the Arkites, the Sinites, the Arvadites, the Zemarites, and the Hamathites.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Before the line narrows it widens. Seventy-odd names cover the whole known world — Japheth to the north and west, Ham to the south — peoples the reader would have met on a wharf or paid a tax to. Sidon and Egypt and Canaan are here, and so are the Philistines, named inside a parenthesis (v. 12) as though four centuries of Israel's grief were a footnote.

A small people surrounded by larger ones is always under pressure to define itself against them. The Chronicler will not allow it. Before Israel is a nation at all, it is a branch. The families in these twelve verses are not the enemy; they are relatives.

One man is given a sentence of his own. He was the first on earth to be a mighty man (v. 10) — Nimrod, whose kingdom in Genesis begins at Babel and takes in Babylon (Gen. 10:8-10). The reader has just walked home from there. The first empire in Scripture and the empire that carried off his grandparents are the same story, and the Chronicler files it under a name in a list and adds nothing.

That restraint is itself the argument. Babel is given one verse. The line that runs to David is given nine chapters.

verseByVerse.quote: The sons of Shem: Elam, Asshur, Arpachshad, Lud, and Aram. And the sons of Aram: Uz, Hul, Gether, and Meshech. Arpachshad fathered Shelah, and Shelah fathered Eber. To Eber were born two sons: the name of the one was Peleg (for in his days the earth was divided), and his brother's name was Joktan. Joktan fathered Almodad, Sheleph, Hazarmaveth, Jerah, Hadoram, Uzal, Diklah, Obal, Abimael, Sheba, Ophir, Havilah, and Jobab; all these were the sons of Joktan.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The camera swings to Shem and the pace changes. Where Japheth's descendants were handed a paragraph and dropped, Shem's are walked one generation at a time: Arpachshad, Shelah, Eber.

Eber's two sons are the fork in the road. Peleg carries the line; Joktan is given thirteen sons and four verses and is never heard of again. And Peleg carries the only other note of character in the chapter — for in his days the earth was divided (v. 19). Nobody is certain what the clause means; the scattering at Babel is the usual reading, and the name itself means division.

What the Chronicler is establishing is a shape. Two brothers, and the longer list is the one that ends. Scripture does this again and again, and it is never the arithmetic that decides: Ishmael will have twelve princes and Isaac one son who matters, and Esau will have kings before Jacob has a tent.

verseByVerse.quote: Shem, Arpachshad, Shelah; Eber, Peleg, Reu; Serug, Nahor, Terah; Abram, that is, Abraham.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Ten more names, and the second half of a symmetry — ten from Adam to Noah, ten from Shem to Abraham. In twenty-seven verses the Chronicler has come from the first man to the man of the promise without once stopping to tell a story.

Then the line halts on a change of name. Abram, that is, Abraham (v. 27). He assumes his reader knows everything that happened in between — the call out of Ur, the night under the stars, the covenant cut between the pieces, the son given when the body was as good as dead — and retells none of it. He sets the two names side by side and lets the second do the work: exalted father, then father of a multitude, given to a man of seventy-five who had no child at all.

The whole book will turn on that habit. God changes what a man is called, and then spends centuries making the name true.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 28–42 — The Brothers Named and Set Aside
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Abraham's sons are given in birth order and then the son who is not the heir is honoured first: Ishmael's twelve princes by name (vv. 29-31), Keturah's six sons and Midian's five after them (vv. 32-33). Only then does the text return to Isaac, and it names his sons without a syllable about the struggle between them — Esau and Israel (v. 34), the new name set down as though it had always been there. Esau's own line and the Horite clans of Seir take a further eight verses (vv. 35-42), including Timna, who appears twice and is the mother of Amalek (vv. 36, 39).
verseByVerse.theology: The pattern is election by narrowing, and it runs the whole length of Scripture: the longer list is the one that ends. But the ones outside the line are not left with nothing. God gave Ishmael princes because he had promised to, and Esau a kingdom, and Keturah's sons a country apiece. Election has never meant that the others are robbed.
verseByVerse.examples: Everything Jacob suffered for his name — the stolen blessing, the twenty years with Laban, the night at the ford — is compressed here into a single word. That is what a genealogy does with a life, and the word it keeps is the one God gave him.

verseByVerse.quote: The sons of Abraham: Isaac and Ishmael. These are their genealogies: the firstborn of Ishmael, Nebaioth, and Kedar, Adbeel, Mibsam, Mishma, Dumah, Massa, Hadad, Tema, Jetur, Naphish, and Kedemah. These are the sons of Ishmael. The sons of Keturah, Abraham's concubine: she bore Zimran, Jokshan, Medan, Midian, Ishbak, and Shuah. The sons of Jokshan: Sheba and Dedan. The sons of Midian: Ephah, Epher, Hanoch, Abida, and Eldaah. All these were the descendants of Keturah.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Here is the pattern that governs the rest of the chapter. Abraham's sons are named in the order of birth, and then the Chronicler takes the son who is not the heir and gives him his full honours first. Ishmael's twelve princes are set down by name, which is a promise kept (Gen. 17:20) and not a slight. Keturah's six sons follow, and Midian's five after them.

More than twenty men, each of whom became a people, and the text spends six verses on them before it returns to the one it is actually following. This is not padding. It is every debt paid to the brothers before the narrowing begins.

God is not grudging towards the ones outside the line. He gave Ishmael princes because he had said he would, and Esau a kingdom, and Keturah's sons a country apiece. Election has never meant that the others are robbed.

verseByVerse.quote: Abraham fathered Isaac. The sons of Isaac: Esau and Israel.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The sons of Isaac: Esau and Israel.

Not Esau and Jacob. The Chronicler steps over the entire struggle — the bought birthright, the stolen blessing, the twenty years with Laban, the night at the ford — and writes the new name into the verse as though it had always been there. The man wrestled until daybreak for it. Here it costs a word.

That is what a genealogy does with a life. Everything a man suffered is compressed into the name he ends up with, and the name he ends up with is the one God gave him.

verseByVerse.quote: The sons of Esau: Eliphaz, Reuel, Jeush, Jalam, and Korah. The sons of Eliphaz: Teman, Omar, Zepho, Gatam, Kenaz, and of Timna, Amalek. The sons of Reuel: Nahath, Zerah, Shammah, and Mizzah. The sons of Seir: Lotan, Shobal, Zibeon, Anah, Dishon, Ezer, and Dishan. The sons of Lotan: Hori and Hemam; and Lotan's sister was Timna. The sons of Shobal: Alvan, Manahath, Ebal, Shepho, and Onam. The sons of Zibeon: Aiah and Anah. The son of Anah: Dishon. The sons of Dishon: Hemdan, Eshban, Ithran, and Cheran. The sons of Ezer: Bilhan, Zaavan, and Akan. The sons of Dishan: Uz and Aran.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Eight verses on Esau's descendants and on the Horite clans of Seir, the people already in the land Esau settled — two families that merged. The Chronicler has no interest in either for its own sake. He is clearing the ground.

One name in the list carries a history. Timna appears twice, as the concubine who bore Amalek (v. 36) and as Lotan's sister (v. 39). Amalek is the nation that cut down the stragglers at the back of the column on the way out of Egypt, and whose king Saul was ordered to destroy and spared. When the genealogies finally end and the first story begins, it is Saul's funeral, and the reason given is a command he did not keep.

Nothing in a list like this is inert. The Chronicler is laying out, in names, the reasons the story afterwards goes the way it goes.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Eight kings are named, each with a city and each handing on to a successor (vv. 43-50), followed by eleven chiefs (vv. 51-54); and the whole roll is dated by one clause — these reigned in Edom before any king reigned over the people of Israel (v. 43). The family outside the promise was governed, settled and crowned while the family inside it was still a tribe of shepherds waiting on a word.
verseByVerse.theology: The verse is written from the far side of the wait, by a man who knows the throne came. It does not say Edom had kings and Israel never would; it dates Edom's kings by Israel's, and so records the delay as a delay rather than as a defeat.
verseByVerse.examples: This is the oldest ache in the life of faith and Scripture never pretends it away: the people who are not waiting on God appear to be doing better, and they appear to be doing better for a long time. Asaph could not resolve it either until he went into the sanctuary.

verseByVerse.quote: These are the kings who reigned in the land of Edom before any king reigned over the people of Israel: Bela the son of Beor, the name of his city being Dinhabah. Bela died, and Jobab the son of Zerah of Bozrah reigned in his place. Jobab died, and Husham of the land of the Temanites reigned in his place. Husham died, and Hadad the son of Bedad, who defeated Midian in the country of Moab, reigned in his place, the name of his city being Avith. Hadad died, and Samlah of Masrekah reigned in his place. Samlah died, and Shaul of Rehoboth on the Euphrates reigned in his place. Shaul died, and Baal-hanan, the son of Achbor, reigned in his place. Baal-hanan died, and Hadad reigned in his place, the name of his city being Pai; and his wife's name was Mehetabel, the daughter of Matred, the daughter of Mezahab.
verseByVerse.commentary:
These are the kings who reigned in the land of Edom before any king reigned over the people of Israel (v. 43).

Read that with the eyes of a man who has no king. Eight of them are then named, each with a city, each dying and handing on — a working succession, generations of it, in the country of the brother who sold his birthright for a bowl of soup. Israel, across those same generations, had nothing of the kind.

The Chronicler neither softens it nor explains it. He records that the family outside the promise was governed, settled and crowned while the family inside it was still a tribe of shepherds waiting on a word.

Then notice what the verse does not say. It does not say Edom had kings and Israel never would. It dates Edom's kings by Israel's — before any king reigned over the people of Israel — and the man writing that clause knows perfectly well that the throne came. The delay is set down as a delay, not as a defeat.

verseByVerse.quote: And Hadad died. The chiefs of Edom were: chiefs Timna, Alvah, Jetheth, Oholibamah, Elah, Pinon, Kenaz, Teman, Mibzar, Magdiel, and Iram; these are the chiefs of Edom.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The kings give way to eleven chiefs, and then Edom is finished. It will return only as an enemy or as a conquered province.

Fifty-four verses have now established one thing: God keeps a record of everyone. Nations, brothers, elder sons, men with cities and crowns — all named, all written down, and none of them the point.

And when the record narrows, in the next chapter, it will narrow to the sons of Israel, and then to Judah, and then to Jesse, and then to a boy nobody thought to call in from the sheep until Samuel asked for him. The God who took the trouble to write down every chief of Edom was working the whole time on a single line, and at the end of it stands a Son whose own genealogy Matthew opens with the two names the Chronicler has just used: the son of David, the son of Abraham.

These are the Kenites who came from Hammath, the father of the house of Rechab.
2.overview:
The twelve tribes are named and then eleven are dropped (vv. 1-2), because this book follows Judah. What follows is the royal genealogy: Judah's disastrous first family (vv. 3-4), Perez and Zerah, Achan (vv. 5-8), the ten silent generations to Jesse (vv. 9-12), and David, last of his brothers, with his two sisters after him (vv. 13-17). The rest of the chapter works outward through Hezron's other households — Caleb, Bezalel, Jair, Jerahmeel, and Sheshan's Egyptian son-in-law (vv. 18-41) — and closes on the towns of Judah, Bethlehem among them, and the Kenite scribes at Jabez (vv. 42-55).

It reads like a filing cabinet and works like an argument. Every objection a returning exile might raise about his own fitness has already been answered by somebody in this list.
2.theology:
The chapter plants the book's thesis inside a name. Broke faith at verse 7 is the verb the Chronicler uses only four times, and each time for a larger subject: a man, two and a half tribes, a king, a nation. The exile is not explained here as bad luck or as Babylonian strength. It is explained as covenant treachery, and the explanation is set down before the story starts.

Against that runs the other line of the chapter: God's stubborn use of the wrong material. A Canaanite wife, a daughter-in-law's deception, a foreign slave, a Moabite quietly omitted here and restored by Matthew. Grace is not a late New Testament development that softens an earlier severity; it is in the register, in the oldest documents Israel had.
2.examples:
Two men in this chapter are recorded because their lines ended (vv. 30, 32), and one is recorded because he stole and was stoned (v. 7). The register is not a list of achievements, and a believer who reads his own life as a ledger of what he has produced is reading the wrong document.

And the thing the chapter is quietly walking towards is a village. Bethlehem is filed in verse 51 between two other villages, with no star over it and no angels above it, because the God who arranges these things was a thousand years from finishing and had already written down the address.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–17 — The Line to David, and What Is in It
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The twelve sons of Israel are named in a single breath (vv. 1-2) and then eleven of them are dropped, because the Chronicler is following one. Judah's line begins badly: a Canaanite wife, a firstborn whom God put him to death for wickedness, and an heir born to Judah by his own daughter-in-law (vv. 3-4). Achan stands in it four verses later as the troubler of Israel (v. 7). Then the ten quiet names that carry everything — Ram, Amminadab, Nahshon, Salmon, Boaz, Obed, Jesse (vv. 10-12) — and Jesse's sons, with David last (vv. 13-15) and his two sisters after him (vv. 16-17).
verseByVerse.theology: The Chronicler is not embarrassed by this line and does not clean it. Election runs through a Canaanite mother, an executed son, a scandal at Timnah and a thief at Jericho, and arrives at a shepherd nobody counted. Matthew, opening the same line, will keep Tamar in it on purpose.
verseByVerse.examples: A believer who thinks his family history disqualifies him has not read a genealogy properly. This one is the royal line of the Son of God, and there is a dead man in verse 3 and a stoning in verse 7.

verseByVerse.quote: These are the sons of Israel: Reuben, Simeon, Levi, Judah, Issachar, Zebulun, Dan, Joseph, Benjamin, Naphtali, Gad, and Asher.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Twelve names, and then eleven of them are set aside. The Chronicler gives the sons of Israel in one breath and immediately follows Judah, who was fourth in birth order and neither the eldest nor the favourite.

He will explain himself three chapters on: Reuben forfeited the birthright, Joseph received the double portion, and the ruler came from Judah. Here he simply does it, and lets the reader notice that the order of the list and the order of the story are not the same. Being first in a family has never yet decided anything in this book.

verseByVerse.quote: The sons of Judah: Er, Onan and Shelah; these three Bath-shua the Canaanite bore to him. Now Er, Judah's firstborn, was evil in the sight of the LORD, and he put him to death. His daughter-in-law Tamar also bore him Perez and Zerah. Judah had five sons in all.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Five verses into the royal genealogy and there is already a corpse. Judah's firstborn was evil in the sight of the LORD, and he put him to death. Not a battle, not an illness — a sentence. And the mother of those first three sons is named as well: Bath-shua the Canaanite, a woman from the people Israel was told not to marry into.

Then the line goes on, and it goes on through Tamar — the daughter-in-law who, when Judah refused her the third son he had promised, sat by the road in a veil and got from him what she had been denied. The two boys born of that night are Perez and Zerah, and Perez carries the crown.

The Chronicler could have started at verse 5. He does not. He writes the Canaanite wife and the executed son and the daughter-in-law into the opening lines of the family that produces the Messiah, and adds no apology and no explanation.

A thousand years later Matthew will do exactly the same thing, and will put Tamar's name in his first paragraph where no genealogy of that era would have put a woman at all (Matt. 1:3). Neither writer is embarrassed. The line is not clean, and the God at the end of it did not come to a clean line.

verseByVerse.quote: The sons of Perez: Hezron and Hamul. The sons of Zerah: Zimri, Ethan, Heman, Calcol, and Dara, five in all. The son of Carmi: Achan, the troubler of Israel, who broke faith in the matter of the devoted thing; and Ethan's son was Azariah.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Four verses of names, and one of them is a bomb. The son of Carmi: Achan, the troubler of Israel, who broke faith in the matter of the devoted thing (v. 7).

The man is in the register because he belongs to the family, and the Chronicler will not remove him. But he does something more deliberate than that. The phrase broke faith translates a verb that this book uses exactly four times in twenty-nine chapters, and the four together are its whole diagnosis of Israel's history: Achan here; the tribes across the Jordan who broke faith with the God of their fathers (5:25); Judah carried to Babylon because of their breach of faith (9:1); and Saul, whose obituary reads So Saul died for his breach of faith (10:13).

A thief at Jericho, two and a half tribes, a king, and finally the whole nation. The same word each time. The Chronicler has planted the thesis of his book inside a list of names, four verses after the genealogy of the Messiah begins, and he never states it as a thesis at all.

verseByVerse.quote: The sons of Hezron that were born to him: Jerahmeel, Ram, and Chelubai. Ram fathered Amminadab, and Amminadab fathered Nahshon, prince of the sons of Judah. Nahshon fathered Salmon, Salmon fathered Boaz, Boaz fathered Obed, Obed fathered Jesse.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Four verses, seven names, and nothing said about any of them except who their fathers were. Ram, Amminadab, Nahshon, Salmon, Boaz, Obed, Jesse. Nahshon is given a title — prince of the sons of Judah — and the rest are given nothing.

These are the centuries between the promise and the throne, and they are handled in twenty-six words. Everything in them happened to somebody: Nahshon stood at the edge of the sea, Salmon lived through the conquest, Boaz got up one morning and went to the gate to settle a matter about a foreign widow. The register keeps the fact and drops the story.

And it drops one story in particular. Boaz is here; Ruth is not. The Chronicler names the man and leaves out the Moabite woman without whom there is no Obed, no Jesse, no David. Matthew, again, will put her back (Matt. 1:5).

What the two lists do together is the point. God's work in a family is carried by generations who are given no lines to speak, and the God who required none of them to be remarkable brought his own Son out of them.

verseByVerse.quote: Jesse fathered Eliab his firstborn, Abinadab the second, Shimea the third, Nethanel the fourth, Raddai the fifth, Ozem the sixth, David the seventh. And their sisters were Zeruiah and Abigail. The sons of Zeruiah: Abishai, Joab, and Asahel, three. Abigail bore Amasa, and the father of Amasa was Jether the Ishmaelite.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesse's sons are counted off and the counting stops early: Ozem the sixth, David the seventh. But 1 Samuel says Jesse had eight sons (1 Sam. 17:12), and has seven of them pass before Samuel before the prophet asks whether that is all and is told There remains yet the youngest, but behold, he is keeping the sheep (1 Sam. 16:11). Seven brothers plus David makes eight, and here David himself is the seventh.

The plain answer is that one son died without children, and a genealogy is not a family photograph. It is a record of descent, and a man who leaves no descendants leaves no entry. This chapter has already noted two such men by name (vv. 30, 32). The Chronicler is not correcting Samuel and not contradicting him; he is doing a different job with the same family.

Then verse 16, which quietly explains a great deal of what comes later. Zeruiah and Abigail are Jesse's daughters — David's sisters. So Joab, Abishai and Asahel are the king's nephews, and so is Amasa, whom Joab will murder. The hardest men in David's reign, the ones he could neither control nor dismiss, were family.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 18–41 — Hezron's Other Houses, and an Egyptian Slave
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The text leaves the royal line and works through Hezron's other sons. Caleb's household produces Hur, and Hur produces Uri, and Uri produces Bezalel (v. 20) — the man who built the tabernacle. Hezron marries Machir's daughter at sixty and fathers Segub, whose son Jair holds twenty-three cities until Geshur and Aram take them (vv. 21-23). Then nine verses on Jerahmeel, Hezron's firstborn, whose line simply stops — twice the register notes a man who died childless (vv. 30, 32). And then Sheshan, who had no sons, only daughters, gives his daughter to Jarha his Egyptian slave, and thirteen generations come out of it (vv. 34-41).
verseByVerse.theology: God's covenant is with a family, and a family is not a pure line. An Egyptian slave marries into the tribe of the Messiah and his descendants are counted, named and kept for four hundred years. The wall between Israel and the nations was never as high as Israel kept trying to build it.
verseByVerse.examples: Two men here died childless and are written down anyway. The register does not only record what continued; it records what ended, and it does not treat the ending as a disgrace.

verseByVerse.quote: Caleb the son of Hezron fathered children by his wife Azubah, and by Jerioth; and these were her sons: Jesher, Shobab, and Ardon. When Azubah died, Caleb married Ephrath, who bore him Hur. Hur fathered Uri, and Uri fathered Bezalel. Afterward Hezron went in to the daughter of Machir the father of Gilead, whom he married when he was sixty years old, and she bore him Segub. And Segub fathered Jair, who had twenty-three cities in the land of Gilead. But Geshur and Aram took from them Havvoth-jair, Kenath, and its villages, sixty towns. All these were descendants of Machir, the father of Gilead. After the death of Hezron, Caleb went in to Ephrathah, the wife of Hezron his father, and she bore him Ashhur, the father of Tekoa.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The text steps off the royal line to follow Hezron's other households, and in the middle of them, three generations down from Caleb, sits a name the reader of Exodus knows: Uri fathered Bezalel (v. 20).

Bezalel is the man God filled with his Spirit to design the tabernacle — the first person in Scripture said to be filled with the Spirit of God, and he was filled in order to work gold and cut stone. He belongs to the tribe the temple builder will come from, and the Chronicler, whose whole book is heading towards a temple, files him here without remark.

Around him is ordinary loss. Hezron marries at sixty and has a son. That son's son holds twenty-three towns in Gilead, and then Geshur and Aram take them (v. 23). Three verses cover an inheritance won and an inheritance lost, and no one says whether it was deserved.

verseByVerse.quote: The sons of Jerahmeel, the firstborn of Hezron: Ram, his firstborn, Bunah, Oren, Ozem, and Ahijah. Jerahmeel also had another wife, whose name was Atarah; she was the mother of Onam. The sons of Ram, the firstborn of Jerahmeel: Maaz, Jamin, and Eker. The sons of Onam: Shammai and Jada. The sons of Shammai: Nadab and Abishur. The name of Abishur's wife was Abihail, and she bore him Ahban and Molid. The sons of Nadab: Seled and Appaim; and Seled died childless. The son of Appaim: Ishi. The son of Ishi: Sheshan. The son of Sheshan: Ahlai. The sons of Jada, Shammai's brother: Jether and Jonathan; and Jether died childless. The sons of Jonathan: Peleth and Zaza. These were the descendants of Jerahmeel.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Nine verses on Jerahmeel, and Jerahmeel was Hezron's firstborn. The line is traced carefully — wives, sons, brothers — and then it simply stops. No king comes out of it, no prophet, no city.

Twice in nine verses the register pauses on the same fact. Seled died childless (v. 30). Jether died childless (v. 32). In a document whose entire purpose is descent, two men are written down precisely because their lines ended.

That is not a small kindness. A genealogy could have passed over them in silence and nobody would ever have known. Instead somebody wrote their names, and the reason given for the entry is the thing that made them, by the book's own logic, unnecessary. God's record of a man is not a record of his usefulness.

verseByVerse.quote: Now Sheshan had no sons, only daughters, but Sheshan had an Egyptian slave whose name was Jarha. So Sheshan gave his daughter in marriage to Jarha his slave, and she bore him Attai. Attai fathered Nathan, and Nathan fathered Zabad. Zabad fathered Ephlal, and Ephlal fathered Obed. Obed fathered Jehu, and Jehu fathered Azariah. Azariah fathered Helez, and Helez fathered Eleasah. Eleasah fathered Sismai, and Sismai fathered Shallum. Shallum fathered Jekamiah, and Jekamiah fathered Elishama.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now Sheshan had no sons, only daughters — and what follows is one of the strangest paragraphs in the genealogies.

Sheshan has an Egyptian slave named Jarha. He gives his daughter to the slave in marriage, and the son of that marriage, Attai, begins a line that the Chronicler then traces for thirteen generations, one careful verse at a time, longer and more patiently than he traces most of Judah.

Consider what is in the register. A man of Judah with no heir. A foreigner from the nation of the brick pits. A slave, given his master's daughter and his master's future. And the whole tribe of the Messiah keeps the record of his descendants as carefully as it keeps its own.

Israel spent much of its history arguing about who was properly inside. Its own family papers, kept in the temple and copied by scribes, say that a slave out of Egypt married into the royal tribe and his children were counted. The door was never as narrow as the doorkeepers wanted.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 42–55 — Caleb, Bethlehem, and the Scribes at Jabez
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Caleb's descendants are traced through towns rather than through sons: Ziph, Hebron, Maon, Beth-zur, Madmannah (vv. 42-49), and Achsah, his daughter, who in Joshua asked her father for springs of water (v. 49). Hur's line gives Kiriath-jearim and, in one clause that the whole Bible leans on, Salma, the father of Bethlehem (v. 51). The chapter closes on the clans of scribes at Jabez, who turn out not to be Israelites at all but Kenites (v. 55).
verseByVerse.theology: Bethlehem enters the record here as a name in a list, four hundred years before Micah names it and a thousand before the birth. Providence lays its groundwork in places nobody is watching, and the town that will hold the manger is filed among the towns of Judah without a word of comment.
verseByVerse.examples: The men who kept Israel's written records were, by the Chronicler's own note, descended from Kenites. The people preserving the book were not born inside the nation whose book it was.

verseByVerse.quote: The sons of Caleb the brother of Jerahmeel: Mareshah his firstborn, who fathered Ziph. The son of Mareshah: Hebron. The sons of Hebron: Korah, Tappuah, Rekem and Shema. Shema fathered Raham, the father of Jorkeam; and Rekem fathered Shammai. The son of Shammai: Maon; and Maon fathered Beth-zur. Ephah also, Caleb's concubine, bore Haran, Moza, and Gazez; and Haran fathered Gazez. The sons of Jahdai: Regem, Jotham, Geshan, Pelet, Ephah, and Shaaph. Maacah, Caleb's concubine, bore Sheber and Tirhanah. She also bore Shaaph the father of Madmannah, Sheva the father of Machbenah and the father of Gibea; and the daughter of Caleb was Achsah. These were the descendants of Caleb. The sons of Hur the firstborn of Ephrathah: Shobal the father of Kiriath-jearim,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Caleb's descendants are given as towns as much as as people: Ziph, Hebron, Jorkeam, Maon, Beth-zur, Madmannah, Machbenah, Gibea. This is a survey as much as a genealogy — who holds what, and by what right.

To a community that had just come home to a land other people had been farming for seventy years, that was not antiquarian. It was the deed to the farm. A returning family could put a finger on a verse and say: this ridge, these terraces.

And at the end of the list, one daughter. The daughter of Caleb was Achsah (v. 49) — the woman who, given a field in the Negeb, asked her father for the springs as well, and got them. She is remembered for asking for water in a dry place, which is not the worst thing to be remembered for.

verseByVerse.quote: Salma, the father of Bethlehem, and Hareph the father of Beth-gader. Shobal the father of Kiriath-jearim had other sons: Haroeh, half of the Menuhoth. And the clans of Kiriath-jearim: the Ithrites, the Puthites, the Shumathites, and the Mishraites; from these came the Zorathites and the Eshtaolites. The sons of Salma: Bethlehem, the Netophathites, Atroth-beth-joab and half of the Manahathites, the Zorites. The clans also of the scribes who lived at Jabez: the Tirathites, the Shimeathites and the Sucathites. These are the Kenites who came from Hammath, the father of the house of Rechab.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Hur's line runs out into the villages of Judah, and one of them stops the eye. Salma, the father of Bethlehem (v. 51).

That is all. A name, a town, and on to Beth-gader. Bethlehem enters the Bible's records here as an entry in a survey of Judah — a small place, unremarkable enough that Micah will have to call it too little to be among the clans of Judah before promising that the ruler comes out of it. Four hundred years before the prophecy and a thousand before the night, the town is on the list and nobody is watching it.

The last verse is stranger still. The scribes lived at Jabez, and the scribes were Kenites — the people of Jethro, Moses' father-in-law, and not Israelites at all. The men who kept the written record of the covenant nation had come in from outside it.

So the chapter that began with a Canaanite mother ends with foreign scribes, and between them stand an executed son, a thief, an Egyptian slave and a town too small to count. This is the line God chose, and kept, and came down into. He was never looking for material he could be proud of. He was making something he could be glorified in.

3.title: The House of David: The Covenant Line Continues
3.text: <sup>1</sup>These are the sons of David who were born to him in Hebron: the firstborn, Amnon, by Ahinoam the Jezreelite; the second, Daniel, by Abigail the Carmelite,<sup>2</sup>the third, Absalom, whose mother was Maacah, the daughter of Talmai, king of Geshur; the fourth, Adonijah, whose mother was Haggith;<sup>3</sup>the fifth, Shephatiah, by Abital; the sixth, Ithream, by his wife Eglah;<sup>4</sup>six were born to him in Hebron, where he reigned for seven years and six months. And he reigned thirty-three years in Jerusalem.<sup>5</sup>These were born to him in Jerusalem: Shimea, Shobab, Nathan and Solomon, four by Bath-shua, the daughter of Ammiel;<sup>6</sup>then Ibhar, Elishama, Eliphelet,<sup>7</sup>Nogah, Nepheg, Japhia,<sup>8</sup>Elishama, Eliada, and Eliphelet, nine.<sup>9</sup>All these were David's sons, besides the sons of the concubines, and Tamar was their sister.<sup>10</sup>The son of Solomon was Rehoboam, Abijah his son, Asa his son, Jehoshaphat his son,<sup>11</sup>Joram his son, Ahaziah his son, Joash his son,<sup>12</sup>Amaziah his son, Azariah his son, Jotham his son,<sup>13</sup>Ahaz his son, Hezekiah his son, Manasseh his son,<sup>14</sup>Amon his son, Josiah his son.<sup>15</sup>The sons of Josiah: Johanan the firstborn, the second Jehoiakim, the third Zedekiah, the fourth Shallum.<sup>16</sup>The descendants of Jehoiakim: Jeconiah his son, Zedekiah his son;<sup>17</sup>and the sons of Jeconiah, the captive: Shealtiel his son,<sup>18</sup>Malchiram, Pedaiah, Shenazzar, Jekamiah, Hoshama and Nedabiah;<sup>19</sup>and the sons of Pedaiah: Zerubbabel and Shimei; and the sons of Zerubbabel: Meshullam and Hananiah, and Shelomith was their sister;<sup>20</sup>and Hashubah, Ohel, Berechiah, Hasadiah, and Jushab-hesed, five.<sup>21</sup>The sons of Hananiah: Pelatiah and Jeshaiah, his son Rephaiah, his son Arnan, his son Obadiah, his son Shecaniah.<sup>22</sup>The son of Shecaniah: Shemaiah. And the sons of Shemaiah: Hattush, Igal, Bariah, Neariah, and Shaphat, six.<sup>23</sup>The sons of Neariah: Elioenai, Hizkiah, and Azrikam, three.<sup>24</sup>The sons of Elioenai: Hodaviah, Eliashib, Pelaiah, Akkub, Johanan, Delaiah, and Anani, seven.
3.overview:
David's family is set out in three movements: the sons born at Hebron and at Jerusalem, with their mothers, closing on his daughter Tamar (vv. 1-9); the throne handed down from Solomon to Josiah in one unvarying formula, nineteen kings in five verses (vv. 10-14); and then the collapse and what came after it — Josiah's sons, Jeconiah the captive, Zerubbabel, and six further generations of a royal house with no crown (vv. 15-24).

The chapter's weight is in its last verses, and they are the easiest to skim. A king list that keeps being written after the kingdom has fallen is not an administrative record. It is a community refusing to concede that God has finished with a promise.
3.theology:
The covenant with David was unconditional in its promise and painful in its administration. This chapter shows both at once: an unbroken succession through men who in many cases deserved to end it, and then a break in the succession that did not break the line. God does not keep his word by preventing disaster. He keeps it through disaster, which is harder to watch and much harder to doubt afterwards.

The omissions matter too. Uriah is not in verse 5, and the whole of Manasseh's reign is not in verse 13. The Chronicler is not hiding these things — his own second volume tells them — but a genealogy answers one question, and the question is not what the fathers deserved. It is whether the promise survived them.
3.examples:
The last man named in this chapter, Anani, is otherwise unknown. He is the end of the Old Testament's record of the house of David, and he did nothing anyone wrote down. Faithfulness in a family very often looks like that: someone in a bad century keeps the records, teaches the children, and never learns what it was for.

They did learn, eventually. Every clerk who copied these names was working on the genealogy of Jesus of Nazareth, and not one of them knew it.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Six sons born at Hebron, each with his mother named (vv. 1-3), and nine more at Jerusalem (vv. 5-8), with the reign split across the two cities — seven years and six months in Hebron, thirty-three in Jerusalem (v. 4). Four of the Jerusalem sons are by Bath-shua, and Solomon is the last of those four (v. 5). The roll closes with a line that has no business in a list of sons: All these were David's sons, besides the sons of the concubines, and Tamar was their sister (v. 9).
verseByVerse.theology: The Chronicler records the family without narrating it. Amnon, Absalom and Adonijah are here in birth order, and what each of them did to this house is left entirely to the reader who already knows. A register can be merciful in a way a narrative cannot: it tells the truth about who existed without retelling what they did.
verseByVerse.examples: Tamar is named last and given no story. Her brother's crime against her set fire to David's household, and the one thing the register can still do for her is refuse to leave her out.

verseByVerse.quote: These are the sons of David who were born to him in Hebron: the firstborn, Amnon, by Ahinoam the Jezreelite; the second, Daniel, by Abigail the Carmelite, the third, Absalom, whose mother was Maacah, the daughter of Talmai, king of Geshur; the fourth, Adonijah, whose mother was Haggith; the fifth, Shephatiah, by Abital; the sixth, Ithream, by his wife Eglah; six were born to him in Hebron, where he reigned for seven years and six months. And he reigned thirty-three years in Jerusalem.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Six sons, six mothers, one city. The Chronicler gives the Hebron years with the care of a clerk, and three of the names in the list are the reason David's old age was a misery.

Amnon the firstborn raped his half-sister. Absalom the third killed Amnon for it, then took the kingdom, then died in a tree. Adonijah the fourth crowned himself while his father was still breathing. Half the sons born in these three verses tore the house down.

None of that is said. The register gives the names, the mothers and the birth order, and moves on to the arithmetic of the reign: seven years and six months in Hebron, thirty-three in Jerusalem. A man's life reduced to two numbers and a list of children, which is what a genealogy always does and what a funeral usually does too.

The mothers are named because in a royal house the mother is the political fact. Maacah, Absalom's mother, was a foreign princess, the daughter of the king of Geshur — which is where Absalom went when he had to run.

verseByVerse.quote: These were born to him in Jerusalem: Shimea, Shobab, Nathan and Solomon, four by Bath-shua, the daughter of Ammiel; then Ibhar, Elishama, Eliphelet, Nogah, Nepheg, Japhia, Elishama, Eliada, and Eliphelet, nine. All these were David's sons, besides the sons of the concubines, and Tamar was their sister.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Nine sons in Jerusalem, and the first four are by Bath-shua, the daughter of Ammiel. That is Bathsheba, and Solomon is the fourth of her four.

The Chronicler says nothing else. Not the roof, not the letter to Joab, not Uriah, not Nathan, not the week David lay on the ground while the first child died. He records a marriage that produced four sons, one of whom built the temple, and he leaves the crime out of the register entirely.

Matthew will not. Writing the same line, at the same point, he declines the woman's name and writes instead that David was the father of Solomon by the wife of Uriah (Matt. 1:6). One writer keeps the family's record; the other keeps the family's conscience. Scripture gives both, and the reader who has only one of them has half of what happened.

Then the last line of the roll: and Tamar was their sister. She is the only daughter named in the chapter, and she is named after nineteen brothers, and nothing is said about her at all. What was done to her is in another book. Here she is simply counted, which is more than her family managed at the time.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 10–16 — Nineteen Kings in Five Verses
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: From Rehoboam to Josiah the throne of Judah is handed on in a single unbroken formula — his son, his son, his son — nineteen reigns in five verses (vv. 10-14), with no assessment of any of them. Then Josiah's four sons (v. 15), and the collapse: Jehoiakim, and after him Jeconiah his son (v. 16), the king who went to Babylon.
verseByVerse.theology: Everything the books of Kings spend chapters weighing — the high places, the reforms, the murders, the good kings and the disastrous ones — is compressed here into succession alone. The Chronicler is not indifferent to it; he will spend the whole of his second volume on it. Here he is establishing one fact only, and it is the fact the exiles needed: the line held.
verseByVerse.examples: Manasseh is in verse 13 between Hezekiah and Amon, with nothing said about him. The worst king Judah ever had is a name in the middle of a list, which is what happens to every reign eventually.

verseByVerse.quote: The son of Solomon was Rehoboam, Abijah his son, Asa his son, Jehoshaphat his son, Joram his son, Ahaziah his son, Joash his son, Amaziah his son, Azariah his son, Jotham his son, Ahaz his son, Hezekiah his son, Manasseh his son, Amon his son, Josiah his son.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Five verses, nineteen kings, and not one word of judgment on any of them.

Kings and Chronicles will both give these reigns at length elsewhere, weighing each man and naming what he did to the high places. Here the formula never varies: his son, his son, his son. Asa the reformer and Ahaz who burned his children get the same three words. Hezekiah, who prayed and was heard, is a name between Ahaz and Manasseh. Manasseh, who filled Jerusalem with innocent blood, is a name between Hezekiah and Amon.

The flatness is doing something. To a man reading this in a ruined city, the question was not which of his ancestors had been admirable. It was whether the chain had held from Solomon to the fire, and the answer he needed was the one this list gives without adjectives: it did.

God's faithfulness to a promise is not measured by the quality of the people it passes through. If it were, it would have stopped at verse 11.

verseByVerse.quote: The sons of Josiah: Johanan the firstborn, the second Jehoiakim, the third Zedekiah, the fourth Shallum. The descendants of Jehoiakim: Jeconiah his son, Zedekiah his son;
verseByVerse.commentary:
Josiah's four sons, and the succession goes wrong immediately. Johanan is the firstborn and never reigns; the throne goes to the second, then to the fourth, then back to the second's son, then to the third. Judah burned through four kings in twenty-two years, and three of them were brothers.

Josiah was the best king since David and he died at Megiddo with an arrow in him, and these are his sons. Nothing about a good father guarantees the generation after him. The Chronicler sets the four names down and lets the reader count how quickly it all came apart.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 17–24 — The Line That Keeps Going After the Throne Is Gone
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Jeconiah is given a title rather than a kingdom — the sons of Jeconiah, the captive (v. 17) — and from there the register does something no other royal genealogy in the ancient world does. It carries on. Shealtiel, Pedaiah, Zerubbabel who rebuilt the temple (v. 19), and then six further generations of men who never ruled anything, down to seven brothers of whom the last is named Anani (vv. 21-24).
verseByVerse.theology: A king list is normally kept because there is a throne to claim. This one is kept for generations after the throne is gone, by people with no political prospect whatever, because the promise made to David was not conditional on his descendants holding office. The register is an act of faith in a covenant, maintained by clerks.
verseByVerse.examples: The last name in the chapter belongs to a man about whom nothing at all is known. The line does not end in a blaze; it trails off into obscurity — and stays alive there for four hundred years until an angel finds a carpenter of that house.

verseByVerse.quote: and the sons of Jeconiah, the captive: Shealtiel his son, Malchiram, Pedaiah, Shenazzar, Jekamiah, Hoshama and Nedabiah; and the sons of Pedaiah: Zerubbabel and Shimei; and the sons of Zerubbabel: Meshullam and Hananiah, and Shelomith was their sister; and Hashubah, Ohel, Berechiah, Hasadiah, and Jushab-hesed, five.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The sons of Jeconiah, the captive. The word is a title now. He was eighteen when he surrendered Jerusalem, he spent thirty-seven years in a Babylonian prison, and the register of the house of David identifies him by his captivity.

And then the line does not stop. Shealtiel. Pedaiah. Zerubbabel — the man who came home with the first company and laid the foundation of the second temple while old men who remembered the first one wept out loud.

There is a difficulty in the verse and it is better named than skated. Here Zerubbabel is the son of Pedaiah; Ezra, Haggai and Matthew all call him the son of Shealtiel. The likeliest explanation is the one the law provided for exactly this case: Shealtiel died without a son, his brother Pedaiah raised up an heir to his name, and Zerubbabel was legally the one man's son and biologically the other's. Ancient genealogies record legal descent, not only blood, and a returning community would have known which was which.

verseByVerse.quote: The sons of Hananiah: Pelatiah and Jeshaiah, his son Rephaiah, his son Arnan, his son Obadiah, his son Shecaniah. The son of Shecaniah: Shemaiah. And the sons of Shemaiah: Hattush, Igal, Bariah, Neariah, and Shaphat, six. The sons of Neariah: Elioenai, Hizkiah, and Azrikam, three. The sons of Elioenai: Hodaviah, Eliashib, Pelaiah, Akkub, Johanan, Delaiah, and Anani, seven.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Four more verses, and this is where the chapter has been going.

After Zerubbabel the register keeps writing. Hananiah, Pelatiah, Rephaiah, Arnan, Obadiah, Shecaniah, Shemaiah, Neariah, Elioenai — and then seven brothers, the last of whom is Anani. Six generations past the last event the Old Testament records, in a family that had not held power for centuries, somebody was still keeping the papers of the house of David.

Consider what that took. No throne, no army, no realistic prospect, and a Persian governor in the citadel. Every reason to let the record lapse, and one reason not to: God had said of David's son I will establish his throne forever, and men who could see no evidence of it went on writing down the names anyway.

They were right to. Four centuries after Anani, a young woman in Nazareth was told that the Lord God would give her son the throne of his father David, and Matthew opened his Gospel by running this same list forward — Jechoniah, Shealtiel, Zerubbabel — until it arrived at a carpenter and stopped. The clerks who kept this chapter going in the dark were keeping the address of the King.

4.overview:
The chapter runs Judah a second time by clans rather than by kings (vv. 1-23), and then gives Simeon his own short record (vv. 24-43). In the middle of Judah's clans the list halts for two verses on a man called Jabez, who prays and is answered (vv. 9-10) — the only prayer, and the only recorded act of God, in nine chapters of names.

Around him the section fills with people the narrative books never mention: an Egyptian princess married into the tribe (v. 17), houses of linen workers and potters (vv. 21-23), a fading tribe that kept its records anyway (v. 33), and five hundred men who finished a war Saul had abandoned (vv. 42-43).
4.theology:
Jabez is the doctrinal centre and is easily mishandled in both directions. It is not a formula, and the surrounding verses prove it: the chapter is full of men who received no enlargement. Nor is it a curiosity to be embarrassed by. God is presented here exactly as the rest of Scripture presents him — able to be asked, and pleased to answer — and the answer is recorded in the one document least likely to invent it.

The second theme is providence working through decline. Simeon shrinks, loses its towns, and is absorbed; and in the same breath its princes increase and its men complete an unfinished command of God. A tribe going down is not therefore a tribe God has finished using.
4.examples:
A reader who was handed the Jabez prayer as a method and found that his own borders did not move has been badly served, and the cure is in the chapter rather than in a rebuke. Jabez asked for a specific thing out of a specific pain, and rested it all on that your hand might be with me. A prayer built on that clause can survive not getting what it asked for. A prayer built on the enlargement cannot.

And the man whose name meant pain, who asked to be kept from it, has a descendant who was named before birth as the one who would save his people from their sins, and who asked in a garden to be kept from what was coming, and was not.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–10 — Judah's Clans, and the Prayer of Jabez
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Judah's line is worked through a second time, sideways — Shobal, Hur, Ashhur of Tekoa and their households (vv. 1-8), with Hur named again as the father of Bethlehem (v. 4). Then the list stops dead for two verses. A man named for his mother's pain prays one sentence, and the register records that God granted what he asked (vv. 9-10).
verseByVerse.theology: This is the only prayer in nine chapters of names, and the only place in them where God is said to do anything. The Chronicler puts it in the middle of a land survey, which is where it belongs: a man asking for a border in a chapter about who holds what.
verseByVerse.examples: Jabez is defined at birth by somebody else's suffering, and he takes that name to God rather than to a mirror. What he asks for is not escape from the name but blessing inside it.

verseByVerse.quote: The sons of Judah: Perez, Hezron, Carmi, Hur, and Shobal. Reaiah the son of Shobal fathered Jahath, and Jahath fathered Ahumai and Lahad. These were the clans of the Zorathites. These were the sons of Etam: Jezreel, Ishma, and Idbash; and the name of their sister was Hazzelelponi, and Penuel fathered Gedor, and Ezer fathered Hushah. These were the sons of Hur, the firstborn of Ephrathah, the father of Bethlehem. Ashhur, the father of Tekoa, had two wives, Helah and Naarah; Naarah bore him Ahuzzam, Hepher, Temeni, and Haahashtari. These were the sons of Naarah. The sons of Helah: Zereth, Izhar, and Ethnan. Koz fathered Anub, Zobebah, and the clans of Aharhel, the son of Harum.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Judah again, from a different angle. The Chronicler has already run the royal line; now he works across the tribe sideways, clan by clan and town by town — Zorathites, the sons of Etam, Ashhur of Tekoa and his two wives.

Bethlehem surfaces a second time in eight verses (v. 4), still with no weight on it, still a village belonging to Hur. And a sister is named in verse 3, Hazzelelponi, one of the handful of women in these lists, with nothing recorded about her but the fact that she existed and somebody knew her name.

This is what most of a nation's history looks like from the inside: households, villages, a trade, a well. The men who make it into the narrative books are a fraction of a per cent of the people God was actually dealing with.

verseByVerse.quote: Jabez was more honorable than his brothers; and his mother called his name Jabez, saying, "Because I bore him in pain." Jabez called upon the God of Israel, saying, "Oh that you would bless me and enlarge my border, and that your hand might be with me, and that you would keep me from harm so that it might not bring me pain!" And God granted what he asked.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Nine chapters of names, and here the list stops and a man speaks.

Jabez was more honorable than his brothers; and his mother called his name Jabez, saying, Because I bore him in pain. He is introduced by somebody else's suffering. Whatever happened at that birth, it was bad enough that the woman named the child after it, and he carried the word for pain every time anyone called him to dinner.

What he does with it is the point. Oh that you would bless me and enlarge my border, and that your hand might be with me, and that you would keep me from harm so that it might not bring me pain! Four requests, and the last of them turns his own name back on God: keep me from the thing I am called.

The middle two are the substance. Enlarge my border is not a slogan about ambition; it sits in a chapter of land allocations, and it is a farmer asking for ground. That your hand might be with me is what the request rests on, and it is the one petition that makes the other three safe to pray.

This prayer has been sold as a technique, and the chapter it lives in refuses that reading. Around Jabez are dozens of men who are given no prayer, no answer and no enlargement, and the register does not suggest they failed to say the words. What is recorded here is not a formula that works. It is that a man in pain asked the God of Israel for something specific, and the God of Israel is the kind of God who is asked.

And God granted what he asked. Five words, in the middle of a list that has granted nothing to anyone, and the God of nine chapters of silent record-keeping turns out to have been listening the whole time.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 11–23 — Craftsmen, Potters, and Pharaoh's Daughter
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The clans run on through Kenaz and Othniel the judge (v. 13), through a valley of craftsmen (v. 14), and through Caleb the son of Jephunneh (v. 15). In the middle of them sits a marriage nobody explains: Mered took Bithiah, the daughter of Pharaoh (v. 17). The section closes with two trades — the houses of the linen workers at Beth-ashbea (v. 21), and the potters who lived at Netaim and Gederah and worked in the king's service (v. 23).
verseByVerse.theology: An Egyptian princess is married into the tribe of the Messiah and given a Hebrew name meaning daughter of the LORD. Two chapters earlier an Egyptian slave married into the same tribe. The Chronicler notes both and argues from neither; he simply will not let the record be tidier than the family was.
verseByVerse.examples: The last men named in the section are potters, and they are named. Whole clans of Judah are remembered for linen and clay rather than for battles, and the register does not rank them below the princes it has just listed.

verseByVerse.quote: Chelub, the brother of Shuhah, fathered Mehir, who fathered Eshton. Eshton fathered Beth-rapha, Paseah, and Tehinnah, the father of Ir-nahash. These are the men of Recah. The sons of Kenaz: Othniel and Seraiah; and the sons of Othniel: Hathath and Meonothai. Meonothai fathered Ophrah; and Seraiah fathered Joab, the father of Ge-harashim, so-called because they were craftsmen. The sons of Caleb the son of Jephunneh: Iru, Elah, and Naam; and the son of Elah: Kenaz. The sons of Jehallelel: Ziph, Ziphah, Tiria, and Asarel. The sons of Ezrah: Jether, Mered, Epher, and Jalon. These are the sons of Bithiah, the daughter of Pharaoh, whom Mered married; and she conceived and bore Miriam, Shammai, and Ishbah, the father of Eshtemoa. And his Judahite wife bore Jered the father of Gedor, Heber the father of Soco, and Jekuthiel the father of Zanoah. The sons of the wife of Hodiah, the sister of Naham, were the fathers of Keilah the Garmite and Eshtemoa the Maacathite. The sons of Shimon: Amnon, Rinnah, Ben-hanan, and Tilon. The sons of Ishi: Zoheth and Ben-zoheth.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The clans continue, and two of them carry weight. Othniel is here (v. 13) — Israel's first judge, the man who took Kiriath-sepher and married Achsah, the woman who asked her father for springs two chapters ago. And a valley is named for its trade: Ge-harashim, so-called because they were craftsmen (v. 14).

Then a marriage with no explanation attached. Mered married Bithiah, the daughter of Pharaoh (v. 17), and she is given a Hebrew name that means daughter of the LORD. Two chapters ago an Egyptian slave married into this tribe. Now an Egyptian princess. The nation that had been the house of bondage keeps supplying wives and husbands to the family of the Messiah, and the Chronicler never once stops to justify it.

He does not need to. The reader who wants a pure line has not been paying attention since chapter 2, verse 3.

verseByVerse.quote: The sons of Shelah the son of Judah: Er the father of Lecah, Laadah the father of Mareshah, and the clans of the house of linen workers at Beth-ashbea; and Jokim, and the men of Cozeba, and Joash, and Saraph, who ruled in Moab and returned to Lehem (now the records are ancient). These were the potters who were inhabitants of Netaim and Gederah. They lived there in the king's service.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Three verses on the descendants of Shelah, and they are remembered by what they made. There were clans of the house of linen workers at Beth-ashbea, and there were potters at Netaim and Gederah who lived there in the king's service.

Weavers and potters, working for the crown, written into the official genealogy of the royal tribe alongside princes and judges. The chapter has just recorded a man whose prayer God answered; it now records men whose whole entry is that they made cloth.

Both are in the same book and neither is ranked. There is a way of reading Scripture that treats the Jabez verse as the important one and the potters as filler, and the Chronicler, who wrote them four verses apart, plainly did not read it that way.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 24–43 — Simeon: The Tribe That Shrank
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Simeon is given his own genealogy and the news is not good: his brothers did not have many children, nor did all their clan multiply like the men of Judah (v. 27). Their towns are listed, with a date on them — these were their cities until David reigned (v. 31). Then two expeditions: princes who went east to Gedor for pasture in Hezekiah's day and took it (vv. 34-41), and five hundred men who went to Mount Seir and destroyed the remnant of the Amalekites who had escaped (vv. 42-43).
verseByVerse.theology: Simeon's decline was pronounced over him before he had a tribe at all: Jacob's last words scattered Simeon and Levi in Israel for what they did at Shechem. Levi's scattering was turned into priesthood. Simeon's was simply absorption. The same sentence fell on two brothers and God did different things with it.
verseByVerse.examples: The chapter ends with a job finished four hundred years late. Amalek entered this book as a name in a genealogy (1:36); Saul was told to end them and did not; and here five hundred Simeonites do it in a single verse, and nobody writes a song about it.

verseByVerse.quote: The sons of Simeon: Nemuel, Jamin, Jarib, Zerah, Shaul; Shallum was his son, Mibsam his son, Mishma his son. The sons of Mishma: Hammuel his son, Zaccur his son, Shimei his son. Shimei had sixteen sons and six daughters; but his brothers did not have many children, nor did all their clan multiply like the men of Judah.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Simeon gets his own genealogy, and it is short, and the reason is given out loud: his brothers did not have many children, nor did all their clan multiply like the men of Judah.

That is a hard sentence to have in your family papers. Judah grew; Simeon did not. One man in the list has sixteen sons and six daughters, and even he cannot lift the average. The tribe is fading while the record is being kept, and the record says so.

Jacob had said it would be like this. His last words scattered Simeon and Levi in Israel for the massacre at Shechem, and both tribes duly lost their footing. Levi was scattered into the priesthood and given the LORD himself as an inheritance. Simeon was scattered into Judah and slowly disappeared. The same word fell on both brothers, and what God did with it was not the same.

verseByVerse.quote: They lived in Beersheba, Moladah, Hazar-shual, Bilhah, Ezem, Tolad, Bethuel, Hormah, Ziklag, Beth-marcaboth, Hazar-susim, Beth-biri, and Shaaraim. These were their cities until David reigned. And their villages were Etam, Ain, Rimmon, Tochen, and Ashan, five cities, along with all their villages that were around these cities as far as Baal. These were their settlements, and they kept a genealogical record.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The towns of Simeon, and a date stamped on them: these were their cities until David reigned. After David the list is historical. Simeon's towns lay inside Judah's territory from the start, and in the end the tribe was absorbed by the neighbour it lived among.

The last thing said about them is that they kept a genealogical record (v. 33). A shrinking tribe, losing its towns and its identity to a larger one, went on writing down who its people were. That is why they are in this chapter at all.

verseByVerse.quote: Meshobab, Jamlech, Joshah the son of Amaziah, Joel, Jehu the son of Joshibiah, son of Seraiah, son of Asiel, Elioenai, Jaakobah, Jeshohaiah, Asaiah, Adiel, Jesimiel, Benaiah, Ziza the son of Shiphi, son of Allon, son of Jedaiah, son of Shimri, son of Shemaiah— these mentioned by name were princes in their clans, and their fathers' houses increased greatly.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Thirteen princes are named, and the reason for naming them is at the end: these mentioned by name were princes in their clans, and their fathers' houses increased greatly.

Increase, in a tribe the text has just said did not increase. The general trend was decline and inside it these households grew. The Chronicler will not let a summary sentence flatten the individual cases, which is a small mercy of the same kind he showed the men who died childless in chapter 2.

verseByVerse.quote: They journeyed to the entrance of Gedor, to the east side of the valley, to seek pasture for their flocks, where they found rich, good pasture, and the land was very broad, quiet, and peaceful, for the former inhabitants there belonged to Ham. These, registered by name, came in the days of Hezekiah, king of Judah, and destroyed their tents and the Meunites who were found there, and marked them for destruction to this day, and settled in their place, because there was pasture there for their flocks. And some of them, five hundred men of the Simeonites, went to Mount Seir, having as their leaders Pelatiah, Neariah, Rephaiah, and Uzziel, the sons of Ishi. And they defeated the remnant of the Amalekites who had escaped, and they have lived there to this day.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Two expeditions close the chapter, and both are about land: men from a tribe with too little of it going out to find some.

The first party went east to Gedor and found what the text calls rich, good pasture, and the land was very broad, quiet, and peaceful, and took it in Hezekiah's day. The second went south to Mount Seir — five hundred men, four leaders named — and defeated the remnant of the Amalekites who had escaped.

That last clause finishes something. Amalek entered this book as a name in a genealogy: Timna bore Amalek to Eliphaz (1:36), and the nation that came from him ambushed Israel on the way out of Egypt, and Saul was ordered to end them and kept the king and the best of the sheep. Generations later, five hundred men of the smallest tribe walk into the hills and finish the job, and there is no song about it and no prophet present.

God's purposes do not lapse when the man commissioned to carry them out refuses. They are handed on, quietly, to people whose names nobody remembers, and they are completed.

5.title: Reuben, Gad, and Manasseh: Faithfulness and Failure East of the Jordan
5.text: <sup>1</sup>The sons of Reuben the firstborn of Israel (for he was the firstborn, but because he defiled his father's couch, his birthright was given to the sons of Joseph the son of Israel, so that he could not be enrolled as the oldest son;<sup>2</sup>though Judah became strong among his brothers and a chief came from him, yet the birthright belonged to Joseph),<sup>3</sup>the sons of Reuben, the firstborn of Israel: Hanoch, Pallu, Hezron, and Carmi.<sup>4</sup>The sons of Joel: Shemaiah his son, Gog his son, Shimei his son,<sup>5</sup>Micah his son, Reaiah his son, Baal his son,<sup>6</sup>Beerah his son, whom Tiglath-pileser king of Assyria carried away into exile; he was a chief of the Reubenites.<sup>7</sup>And his kinsmen by their clans, when the genealogy of their generations was recorded: the chief, Jeiel, and Zechariah,<sup>8</sup>and Bela the son of Azaz, son of Shema, son of Joel, who lived in Aroer, as far as Nebo and Baal-meon.<sup>9</sup>He also lived to the east as far as the entrance of the desert this side of the Euphrates, because their livestock had multiplied in the land of Gilead.<sup>10</sup>And in the days of Saul they waged war against the Hagrites, who fell into their hand. And they lived in their tents throughout all the region east of Gilead.<sup>11</sup>The sons of Gad lived over against them in the land of Bashan as far as Salecah:<sup>12</sup>Joel the chief, Shapham the second, Janai, and Shaphat in Bashan.<sup>13</sup>And their kinsmen according to their fathers' houses: Michael, Meshullam, Sheba, Jorai, Jacan, Zia and Eber, seven.<sup>14</sup>These were the sons of Abihail the son of Huri, son of Jaroah, son of Gilead, son of Michael, son of Jeshishai, son of Jahdo, son of Buz.<sup>15</sup>Ahi the son of Abdiel, son of Guni, was chief in their fathers' houses,<sup>16</sup>and they lived in Gilead, in Bashan and in its towns, and in all the pasturelands of Sharon to their limits.<sup>17</sup>All of these were recorded in genealogies in the days of Jotham king of Judah, and in the days of Jeroboam king of Israel.<sup>18</sup>The Reubenites, the Gadites, and the half-tribe of Manasseh had valiant men who carried shield and sword, and drew the bow, expert in war, 44,760, able to go to war.<sup>19</sup>They waged war against the Hagrites, Jetur, Naphish, and Nodab.<sup>20</sup>And when they prevailed over them, the Hagrites and all who were with them were given into their hands, for they cried out to God in the battle, and he granted their urgent plea because they trusted in him.<sup>21</sup>They carried off their livestock: 50,000 of their camels, 250,000 sheep, 2,000 donkeys, and 100,000 men alive.<sup>22</sup>For many fell, because the war was of God. And they lived in their place until the exile.<sup>23</sup>The members of the half-tribe of Manasseh lived in the land. They were very numerous from Bashan to Baal-hermon, Senir, and Mount Hermon.<sup>24</sup>These were the heads of their fathers' houses: Epher, Ishi, Eliel, Azriel, Jeremiah, Hodaviah, and Jahdiel, mighty warriors, famous men, heads of their fathers' houses.<sup>25</sup>But they broke faith with the God of their fathers, and whored after the gods of the peoples of the land, whom God had destroyed before them.<sup>26</sup>So the God of Israel stirred up the spirit of Pul king of Assyria, the spirit of Tiglath-pileser king of Assyria, and he took them into exile, namely, the Reubenites, the Gadites, and the half-tribe of Manasseh, and brought them to Halah, Habor, Hara, and the river Gozan, to this day.
5.overview:
The two and a half tribes east of the Jordan are recorded together: Reuben, with the explanation of why the firstborn's birthright went elsewhere (vv. 1-10); Gad beside him, with a note that the survey was taken in the eighth century (vv. 11-17); the combined fighting strength and their victory over the Hagrites (vv. 18-22); and half-Manasseh, numerous and famous, ending in idolatry and deportation (vv. 23-26).

The chapter is arranged around a reversal that is easy to read past. Verse 20 records a prayer answered in the middle of a battle. Verse 25 records the same people breaking faith with the God who answered it. Between them lies everything the book has to say about why a nation with such a history ended up in Babylon.
5.theology:
Verse 20 is one of the clearest statements in the Old Testament of how prayer and means work together: 44,760 expert soldiers, and a victory attributed to a cry and a trust. The Chronicler does not resolve the tension because he does not feel one. Human competence is not a rival to divine action; it is one of the ways divine action arrives.

Verse 26 says the same thing about judgment. God stirred up the spirit of a pagan king, and a pagan king did what pagan kings do, and the exile was both an Assyrian policy and a divine act. This is the doctrine the whole book will need when it comes to explain why Jerusalem fell: not that God lost, but that God was doing something.
5.examples:
The hardest verse here for a Christian reader is not verse 25 but verse 20 read alongside it. A man can look back on a time when he cried out and was heard, and treat that memory as evidence about himself. These tribes had exactly such a memory, and it did not hold them for a generation.

What holds is not the memory of an answered prayer but the God who answered it, and he was as present in the deportation as in the victory. The tribes who crossed back over Jordan into Assyrian hands did not stop being his. Their names are in this chapter, written down by a man in Jerusalem centuries after their nation had ceased to exist.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The chapter opens by explaining itself. Reuben was the firstborn, and because he defiled his father's couch, his birthright was given to the sons of Joseph — and yet the ruler came from Judah (vv. 1-2). Reuben's clans are then traced east of the Jordan, ending on a chief named Beerah whom Tiglath-pileser king of Assyria carried away into exile (v. 6), and on the pasture their multiplying livestock pushed them into (vv. 9-10).
verseByVerse.theology: Three things are separated here that are usually confused: the birthright, the double portion, and the throne. Reuben lost all of it by one act. Joseph received the inheritance and Judah the crown, and neither of them was the eldest. Primogeniture is the world's way of ordering a family, and God has overruled it in nearly every generation of this book.
verseByVerse.examples: A single night's sin cost Reuben's descendants a status they never recovered, and the register still names him first out of respect for a birth order that no longer meant anything.

verseByVerse.quote: The sons of Reuben the firstborn of Israel (for he was the firstborn, but because he defiled his father's couch, his birthright was given to the sons of Joseph the son of Israel, so that he could not be enrolled as the oldest son; though Judah became strong among his brothers and a chief came from him, yet the birthright belonged to Joseph),
verseByVerse.commentary:
Two verses of explanation, and they answer a question the book raised three chapters ago without acknowledging it.

Why does a genealogy of Israel start with Judah, who was fourth? Because Reuben, who was first, defiled his father's couch — he slept with his father's concubine — and his birthright went to the sons of Joseph. And yet, the Chronicler adds, the birthright and the crown did not travel together: though Judah became strong among his brothers and a chief came from him, yet the birthright belonged to Joseph.
